blocks.heading: Output method and value added
blocks.text:
The output method adds value added across productive activities. Value added at a stage is its output value less purchased intermediate inputs used for that output. This avoids counting the same input content again at each later stage. The value of final output can embody several earlier stages, so adding every business’s total sales across the chain would overstate the production value being measured.

In the grower-processor-final producer chain, outputs sell for N$60, N$100 and N$160. Assume the grower has no purchased intermediate input in this simplified illustration, the processor buys the N$60 input and the final producer buys the N$100 output. Added values are 60,40 and 60, which sum 160. The final sale is 160, while the incorrect sum of all stage sales is 320. The assumptions are explicit so no missing inputs are silently treated as zero. In a more detailed case, each stage’s supplied intermediate costs must be deducted on the same basis. Do not confuse value added with profit: it can finance several factor rewards, not just the residual return to enterprise. The output method concerns aggregate production measurement rather than whether each firm sold all its production for cash in the period; a fuller accounting task must state how relevant output and inventories are treated. A stage’s purchased intermediate cost must be distinguished from all its factor payments. Deducting wages again when calculating value added from output less intermediate purchases would change the intended measure. The next income step describes how generated value relates to rewards. These are linked accounting views, not arbitrary alternative ways to remove expenses.

blocks.heading: Income method
blocks.text:
The income method adds relevant factor incomes generated by production over the period. In a simple classroom account these may be described through wages, rent, interest and profit, with the measurement basis explicitly stated. The method approaches the activity through rewards rather than adding final purchases. The classification of a payment depends on what generated it, not simply whether someone receives money in a bank account.

Suppose the same simplified activity generates N$90 labour rewards, N$20 land rewards, N$10 capital rewards and N$40 enterprise rewards, with all relevant accounting components included on the exercise’s stated basis. Their sum is N$160. This matches the output-side example because both measure the same production. Adding a transfer of part of one reward to another household would not create another N$ amount of production income. That redistribution changes who receives resources, not the underlying generated total. Actual national accounts involve scope and valuation adjustments, so the simple identity should not be extended to incompatible totals without checking definitions. The teaching point is the route: identify relevant factor rewards, keep the period and basis consistent and avoid double counting. A salary at one firm and profit calculated after the relevant wage deduction can both appear appropriately, while an undefined cash total cannot replace the classification.

blocks.heading: Expenditure method
blocks.text:
The expenditure method adds final spending on domestic production, using relevant consumption, investment, public expenditure and external adjustments. In a common simple representation, final consumption plus investment plus relevant government purchases plus exports minus imports gives domestic expenditure on output. The terms need the exercise’s definitions. A government transfer is not itself a purchase of newly produced output, although the recipient may later spend. Imports are excluded because the production occurred elsewhere, not because imported products have no value.

In the simplified chain where residents purchase all N$160 of final output and there are no other transactions or adjustments, final expenditure is N$160. Adding intermediate purchases of 60 and 100 again would count value already included in the final product. More detailed exercises may include new investment or inventory changes, so production need not be equated mechanically with a firm’s current sales receipts. Use the supplied treatment rather than ignore unsold production by assumption. The output, income and expenditure routes can be reconciled when scope and basis match; they are not three totals to add together. This connects to the purposes and limitations of measurement explained below. A correct calculation labels the resulting aggregate and period, while a correct interpretation explains what it includes and what wider claim still needs evidence. For an expenditure calculation, identify whether a purchase is final for the accounting purpose, not whether a household happens to call it important. Intermediate inputs feed later production, while final uses are treated under the specified framework. Clear boundaries prevent the same purchase being included once as an input and again as an additional final total.
